full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ZZZ, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > H. Title VIII – Crimes Against Persons > 1. All except Arts. 260–261
topics: Elements of statutory rape under Article 266-A(1)(d), as amended by RA 8353
RA 11648 raised the age to 16 but does not retroact against the accused (Art. 22, RPC)
Victim's testimony consistent with medical findings suffices to prove penetration
Minor inconsistencies; denial versus positive identification
No "without eligibility for parole" qualifier; Jugueta damages

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 4. Positive and Negative Evidence

doctrine:
**Statutory rape** under Article 266-A(1)(d) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, requires only that (1) the offended party is under 12 years of age and (2) the accused had carnal knowledge of her, whether or not there was force, threat, intimidation or grave abuse of authority. Consent is immaterial; the only questions are the victim's age and whether carnal knowledge took place (reiterated). A rape victim's straightforward testimony that conforms with the medico-legal findings is enough to prove penetration. Minor inconsistencies between witnesses do not destroy their credibility, and denial cannot prevail over positive identification.

RA 11648 (2022) raised the age for statutory rape to under 16. It added a close-in-age exemption (an age difference of not more than three years, with a sexual act proven consensual, non-abusive and non-exploitative), which does not apply if the victim is under 13, and it did not amend Article 266-B. **Because RA 11648 is not favorable to the accused, it does not retroact (Art. 22, RPC). A rape committed before it took effect is judged under Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353 alone.**

Statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, the phrase "without eligibility for parole" is used only when the death penalty would have been imposed but for RA 9346; otherwise it must be deleted. Under People v. Jugueta, where the penalty is reclusion perpetua (and not death reduced by RA 9346), civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages are PHP 75,000.00 each, with 6% interest per annum from finality.
facts:
ZZZ, who is deaf-mute, was charged with rape under Article 266-A(1)(d) in relation to Article 266-B of the RPC. The Information alleged that on June 17, 2020, in a town in Cotabato, he had carnal knowledge of AAA, a seven-year-old girl born on January 28, 2013.

At about 7:30 a.m. that day, AAA's mother was away getting a rice ration and her father, BBB, was tapping rubber. ZZZ took AAA by the hand and dragged her from the road into her house. He closed the door, pulled down her shorts, knelt behind her as she was made to bend forward, and inserted his penis into her vagina, causing her pain. BBB arrived and saw ZZZ kneeling behind AAA, both naked from the waist down, making push-and-pull movements. ZZZ threw a stone at BBB and fled, but the barangay captain apprehended him and turned him over to the police. The medico-legal examination found a "hymenal laceration on 5 o'clock position [secondary] to vaginal penetration of a blunt object." ZZZ, assisted in court by his mother, denied the charge and claimed he had only gone to the house to drink tuba.

The RTC (January 29, 2021) convicted ZZZ of "qualified rape," sentenced him to reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole, and awarded PHP 100,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. The CA (February 22, 2023) treated "qualified rape" as a typographical slip, since the body of the RTC decision dealt only with statutory rape. It affirmed the conviction, deleted the parole qualifier, and reduced the awards to PHP 75,000.00 each with 6% interest. On appeal, ZZZ pointed to inconsistencies between AAA's and BBB's testimonies on whether he had undressed and whether he made push-and-pull movements, and argued that penile penetration was improbable.
issues: Whether the 2022 amendment of Article 266-A by RA 11648 applies to a rape committed on June 17, 2020.
Whether the prosecution proved the elements of statutory rape beyond reasonable doubt despite the alleged inconsistencies and the claimed absence of penetration.
Whether the penalty and damages imposed by the CA are correct.
ruling:
**1. No, RA 11648 does not apply.** RA 11648 raised the age for statutory rape from under 12 to under 16 (People v. Dalaguet). Its close-in-age exemption does not apply if the victim is under 13, and it left Article 266-B unchanged. Under Article 22 of the RPC, penal laws retroact only insofar as they favor the accused. The crime was committed on June 17, 2020, and the amendment has "no favorable effect" on ZZZ, so the Court applied Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353, before its amendment by RA 11648.

**2. Yes, statutory rape was proved.** The elements are (1) an offended party under 12 years of age and (2) carnal knowledge, regardless of force or intimidation. Consent is immaterial because the law presumes that a child of tender years has no will of her own. AAA's birth certificate showed she was seven. Carnal knowledge was proved by her positive testimony, BBB's eyewitness account, and the medico-legal finding of hymenal laceration. The inconsistencies on whether ZZZ removed his clothes or made push-and-pull movements concern minor details. "[A]s long as the testimonies of the witnesses corroborate one another on material points, minor inconsistencies therein cannot destroy their credibility." Following People v. Gratela, "when a rape victim's straightforward and truthful testimony conforms with the medical findings of the examining doctor, the same is sufficient to support a conviction for rape." ZZZ's denial is self-serving negative evidence and could not prevail over the categorical identification by AAA and BBB.

**3. Yes, the CA's modifications are correct.** Under Article 266-B, as amended by RA 8353, statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, "without eligibility for parole" qualifies reclusion perpetua only when the death penalty is warranted but not imposed because of RA 9346. Otherwise the phrase is unnecessary, since persons sentenced to an indivisible penalty are understood to be ineligible for parole. ZZZ's penalty is reclusion perpetua, not a death penalty reduced by RA 9346, so the phrase was properly deleted. For the same reason, under People v. Jugueta the damages are PHP 75,000.00 each for civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, with 6% interest per annum from finality.
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED, and the CA Decision dated February 22, 2023 in CA-G.R. CR HC No. 02764-MIN was AFFIRMED. ZZZ was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of statutory rape under Article 266-A, paragraph 1(d) of the RPC, as amended by RA 8353, and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 75,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 75,000.00 as exemplary damages, with 6% interest per annum on all awards from finality until full payment.

bar_questions.q: On May 10, 2021, Berto, 30, had sexual intercourse with Lia, his 10-year-old neighbor, inside her house. Lia testified that Berto pulled down her shorts and inserted his penis into her vagina. Her mother, who walked in on them, testified that Berto was fully naked, while Lia said Berto had only unzipped his pants. The medico-legal officer found a fresh hymenal laceration consistent with penetration by a blunt object. Berto argues that (a) the prosecution failed to prove force or intimidation, and (b) the conflicting accounts of how he was dressed destroy the witnesses' credibility. Should Berto be convicted of statutory rape?

alac.answer: Yes. Berto should be convicted of statutory rape.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 266-A(1)(d) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, statutory rape requires only that the offended party is under 12 years of age and that the accused had carnal knowledge of her. Force, threat or intimidation is not necessary, and consent is immaterial. Minor inconsistencies do not destroy credibility when the testimonies agree on material points, and a victim's straightforward testimony that conforms with the medical findings is enough to prove penetration (People v. ZZZ, G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025, citing People v. Gratela).
alac.application: Lia was 10 years old, so the first element is present and the absence of force does not matter. Her testimony that Berto inserted his penis is corroborated by the medico-legal finding of hymenal laceration and by her mother's eyewitness account. Whether Berto was fully naked or had only unzipped his pants is a minor detail that does not affect the material point, which is that he had carnal knowledge of Lia.
alac.conclusion: Berto is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of statutory rape.

bar_questions.q: On June 1, 2020, Dodong, 19, had consensual sexual intercourse with Mia, who was then 13 years and 6 months old. No force, threat, intimidation or abuse of authority was involved. In 2023 the prosecutor charged Dodong with statutory rape, invoking RA 11648 (2022), which raised the age for statutory rape to under 16. (a) Can Dodong be convicted of statutory rape under Article 266-A(1)(d) for the 2020 act? (b) If the same act had been committed after RA 11648 took effect, would Dodong be exempt under its close-in-age proviso?

alac.answer: (a) No. RA 11648 cannot be applied retroactively against him, and under the law in force on June 1, 2020, Mia was not under 12. (b) No. The close-in-age exemption does not apply because their age difference is more than three years.
alac.legal_basis: Article 22 of the Revised Penal Code gives penal laws retroactive effect only insofar as they favor the accused. In People v. ZZZ (G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025), the Court held that RA 11648, which raised the statutory rape age from under 12 to under 16, has no favorable effect on the accused and therefore does not apply to a rape committed before it took effect; the Court applied Article 266-A as amended by RA 8353. As quoted in that decision, RA 11648 provides that there is no criminal liability for carnal knowledge of a person under 16 when the age difference is not more than three years and the act is proven consensual, non-abusive and non-exploitative, but the exception does not apply if the victim is under 13.
alac.application: (a) The act was committed in June 2020, before RA 11648. Applying the amendment would make the act statutory rape when it was not statutory rape at the time it was done, which is unfavorable to Dodong and barred by Article 22. Under the RA 8353 version, statutory rape requires a victim under 12. Mia was 13, and none of the other circumstances in paragraph 1 was present, so Dodong cannot be convicted of statutory rape (without prejudice to liability under any other law whose elements are proved). (b) Had the act been committed after RA 11648, Mia, being under 16, would fall within the statutory rape age. The close-in-age proviso would not help Dodong, because their age difference of more than five years exceeds three years.
alac.conclusion: Dodong cannot be convicted of statutory rape for the 2020 act, and he would not qualify for the close-in-age exemption had the act been committed after RA 11648.

bar_questions.q: The RTC convicted Pablo of the statutory rape of a nine-year-old girl, committed in 2019, and sentenced him to "reclusion perpetua without eligibility for parole." It ordered him to pay PHP 100,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages. No qualifying circumstance was alleged or proved. On appeal, is the RTC's ruling on the penalty and damages correct?

alac.answer: No. The phrase "without eligibility for parole" should be deleted, and each award should be reduced to PHP 75,000.00, with 6% interest per annum from finality.
alac.legal_basis: Statutory rape is punished by reclusion perpetua under Article 266-B of the RPC, as amended by RA 8353. Under A.M. No. 15-08-02-SC, "without eligibility for parole" is used only when the circumstances warrant the death penalty but it is not imposed because of RA 9346. Otherwise the phrase is unnecessary, since persons sentenced to an indivisible penalty are understood to be ineligible for parole. Under People v. Jugueta, where the penalty imposed is reclusion perpetua other than death reduced by RA 9346, civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages are PHP 75,000.00 each (People v. ZZZ, G.R. No. 267815, August 6, 2025).
alac.application: Pablo committed simple statutory rape with no qualifying circumstance, so the proper penalty is plain reclusion perpetua. Death was never warranted, so the parole qualifier must be deleted. For the same reason, the PHP 100,000.00 awards, which apply only when death is reduced to reclusion perpetua, must be reduced to PHP 75,000.00 each, with legal interest of 6% per annum from finality until paid.
alac.conclusion: The judgment should be modified to plain reclusion perpetua, without the parole qualifier, and to PHP 75,000.00 each for civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages.

notes: The fallo cites "Article 226-B," an evident slip for Article 266-B. The RTC's dispositive portion called the crime "qualified rape"; the CA and the Supreme Court treated the conviction as one for statutory rape. Only three Justices took part (Rosario, J., Gesmundo, C.J., and Hernando, J.); Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. The relationship between ZZZ and AAA's family is redacted in the text.
